title: Lesson 22: Cost Management: Token Budgets, Model Tiers, and Predictable Client Pricing
description: Measuring what a single run costs, routing reasoning and mechanical work onto the right model tiers, keeping recurring workloads inside a budget, and turning a measured unit cost into predictable client pricing.

questions.question: Which kind of work belongs in script mode, running no model at all?
options: Client-facing prose where a weaker answer costs more than the tokens saved
Mechanical jobs fully determined by a script, such as threshold checks
Deciding what a report means when the reasoning is non-trivial
Handling a tricky intake reply that needs judgment
questions.explanation: Mechanical jobs belong in script mode, where they cost nothing and cannot drift; putting them on an agent is a common, invisible overspend.

questions.question: Why is switching a model mid-session a cost risk?
options: It forces the job to run twice before it can respond
It disables the usage reporting for the rest of the session
It raises the output-token price for every later message
It discards the cache and re-reads the context in full
questions.explanation: Providers cache the shared prefix at a large discount, and a mid-session model change throws that cache away, which costs the most when the context is long.

questions.question: When turning a measured unit cost into client pricing, what should drive the number?
options: Your labor, with inference budgeted and both put in writing
The inference bill, since that is what varies month to month
The number of features delivered in the current release
The competitor's published per-seat subscription rate
questions.explanation: Inference is a small part of the cost while your labor is the large one, so you price your labor, budget the inference, and state both plus a ceiling.
